judgments.yea_description: Voted for House Bill 103, which added a chapter to Pennsylvania's fish and boat law for at-risk, derelict and abandoned boats. It defined when a boat counts as each of those three, and let a municipality or law enforcement agency investigate and remove one. The owner is responsible for the cost of removal, storage or junking. An owner who ignores a proper notice commits a summary offense, or a third-degree misdemeanor if those costs exceed $2,500. The Pennsylvania House passed this version 148-55; the Senate then tightened the definitions and it became law as Act 28 of 2025.

judgments.yea_description: Voted for House Bill 858, which requires each county's chief assessor to keep a contact list for real property that is not owner-occupied. A buyer must file contact details within 30 days of purchase, and a municipality must collect them whenever it cites a property for a code violation. A business or limited liability company must also name a person with the authority to fix code violations. A municipality may ask for the details only by showing a reasonable need and affirming it will not use them commercially. The list is confidential, and a county may fine an owner up to $500 for knowingly giving false information. The Pennsylvania House passed it 132-71 and it became law.

judgments.yea_description: Voted for Senate Bill 95, which changed the state Pharmacy Act in three ways. A pharmacist must, on request, tell a customer the pharmacy's retail price and the customer's cost share for a brand-name drug and any generic equivalent, plus where to apply for coverage on the state health insurance exchange. A pharmacy that does not comply commits a summary offense carrying a fine of up to $500. Emergency medical services providers may give one sealed naloxone package to a family member or friend of someone who has overdosed, voluntarily and without liability. The State Board of Pharmacy could also issue 180-day provisional licenses to pharmacists already licensed in another state. The Pennsylvania House passed it 126-77 and it became law.

judgments.yea_description: Voted for House Bill 1425, which created a state directory of electronic cigarettes that contain nicotine. Manufacturers must certify their products every year, post a surety bond of at least $50,000 and pay listing fees. Once the directory has been published for 120 days, only listed products may be sold in Pennsylvania. The Attorney General and the Department of Revenue may inspect sellers, levy escalating civil penalties up to license revocation, and destroy contraband at the owner's expense. The same act raised the presumed retailer cost of doing business on cigarettes, which sets the legal minimum retail price, from 7% to 8.5% and then to 9.5%. The Pennsylvania House agreed to the Senate's version 147-56 and it became law.

judgments.yea_description: Voted for Senate Bill 375, which set new defibrillator rules for schools. Within three years, a school that takes part in interscholastic athletics must keep an automated external defibrillator readily accessible for athletes at games and practices, and must develop a cardiac emergency response plan with annual drills. Every school entity must have at least one person trained and certified in CPR and defibrillator use present in each school building on every school day. School nurses, coaches, marching band directors, physical education teachers and athletic trainers must take that training. Up to $2.5 million from the School Safety and Security Fund goes to nonpublic schools for training costs. The Pennsylvania House passed it 141-59 and it became law.
